title: The four books of the Shia
word: The four books of the Shia
hook: al-Kafi, Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, Tahdhib and Istibsar, with their own science of grading

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malik and Ahmad, and your line: early collections. When your character was tested, did it hold? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

For the one who has no jurist at hand. That's the title of a book, put into English: Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih. Tradition says its author wrote it for people who had no scholar nearby to ask, so they could still find what they needed. It's one of a set of four. For several days now we've been walking through the Sunni collections. Shia Muslims also gathered the reports they trusted, through their own chains, checked by their own scholars. Today, their shelf. The four books of the Shia.
screen: `NO JURIST AT HAND.` → `ONE OF A SET OF FOUR.` → `ANOTHER SHELF.`

segments.voice: First, the names. Al-Kafi, the sufficient, compiled by al-Kulayni. Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, by the scholar known as Shaykh al-Saduq. And two by Shaykh al-Tusi: Tahdhib al-Ahkam, the refining of the rulings, and al-Istibsar, a close look at reports that seem to disagree with each other. Four books, three compilers. Second, what's inside. These books carry reports of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and also reports from the Imams of his family, beginning with Ali, whom Twelver Shia Muslims follow as the rightful guides after the Prophet. For Shia Muslims, the Imams are a trusted channel for the Prophet's teaching, so a chain may run through Ja'far al-Sadiq, or his father, back to the Prophet himself. Third, a beginning. Al-Kafi doesn't open with purity or prayer. Its first book is the book of intellect and ignorance: reports about reason, what it's worth, and what it's for. A collection of religion that starts with the mind. Fourth, the grading. Shia scholars have debated how far a report can rest on the book it sits in. Some, known as the Akhbaris, trusted the four books' reports broadly. Others hold that no book is sound cover to cover by its name alone: with their own science of narrators and their own grades, they weigh each report one at a time. Later scholars wrote commentaries that walk through al-Kafi report by report, judging each chain. So the habit this path has followed all week, asking who told whom, runs here too, along its own roads. Sunni and Shia Muslims keep different shelves. Today is about this one, on its own terms.
screen: `FOUR BOOKS, THREE COMPILERS.` · `THE PROPHET, AND THE IMAMS OF HIS FAMILY.` · `AL-KAFI OPENS WITH THE INTELLECT.` · `EACH REPORT WEIGHED ON ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn their names. Settle, and breathe. This time, each name with its meaning. Al-Kafi: the sufficient. Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih: for the one with no jurist at hand. Tahdhib al-Ahkam: the refining of the rulings. Al-Istibsar: a close look at reports that seem to disagree. Then say only the four names, and see if the meanings come back on their own. Then sit with where the first one begins: a book of faith that opens with the mind. Is there a question in your own life you've been avoiding thinking through? Don't solve it. Just name it to yourself, clearly. The bell holds the time.
The four books of the Shia. Al-Kafi, Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, Tahdhib al-Ahkam and al-Istibsar, each report in them weighed by its own chain. Today's word.
screen: `THE FOUR BOOKS OF THE SHIA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: four books. Today, give the question you named ten real minutes of thought, the way al-Kafi gives its first pages to reason. Tomorrow: sacred hadith. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

notes: A Shia (Twelver) Keeper should review this whole day.

Translation of the title Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih as 'for the one who has no jurist at hand', and the tradition that al-Saduq wrote it for people without a scholar nearby (his introduction mentions a request and a medical book of a similar title): confirm.
Al-Istibsar glossed as 'a close look at reports that seem to disagree' (it addresses conflicting reports); Tahdhib al-Ahkam as 'the refining of the rulings': confirm glosses.
Al-Kafi's Usul opens with Kitab al-'Aql wa al-Jahl: confirm.
'Later scholars wrote commentaries that walk through al-Kafi report by report, judging each chain' refers to works such as al-Majlisi's Mir'at al-'Uqul; confirm.
'Four books, three compilers' counts from the titles named (al-Kulayni, al-Saduq, al-Tusi x2): confirm.
Description of the Imams 'beginning with Ali' and 'a trusted channel for the Prophet's teaching': confirm phrasing is acceptable to Twelver scholars; Isma'ili and Zaydi traditions are not covered.
Trapdoor floor one is offered as a common assumption; the lesson does not compare or rank the Sunni and Shia collections.

Editor: the teach, myth, fork and trapdoor no longer say Shia scholars as a whole reject treating the four books as sound throughout; the Akhbari view (broad trust in the four books) is now named beside those who weigh each report.
